summary: This work develops an accelerated radon daughter plateout facility that enhances deposition rates by $7 \times 10^4$ relative to ambient conditions, enabling in situ studies of $^{222}$Rn progeny impacts on superconducting qubits. Simulations and measurements show that $^{210}$Po surface activity from radon plateout can contribute high-energy $\alpha$-decays ($\approx 5.3$ MeV) at rates comparable to cosmic-ray protons in surface labs, and becomes dominant in shielded underground operation.
motivation: Radon daughters plate out onto device surfaces during fabrication and packaging, creating long-lived $^{210}$Pb (half-life 22.2 y) sources of ionizing radiation that produce spatiotemporally correlated qubit errors. As quantum processors scale to larger areas, understanding and mitigating this intrinsic radiation source—impossible to shield against—is essential for fault-tolerant architectures.
method: A closed-loop radon exposure system with a Pylon source and 3.5-liter pressure vessel injected radon at $4{-}7$ MBq/m$^3$ (about $1.8 \times 10^5$ times ambient) for 7-day exposures. Copper test pieces were exposed with and without applied $-63$ V bias to study electric-field enhancement. $^{210}$Po activities were measured via alpha spectroscopy using an Alpha Duo detector, and a dead-air diffusion model was developed to predict plateout rates and project impacts on qubit devices using Geant4 simulations.
result: At $-63$ V bias, copper foils achieved $\mathcal{A}_{3\mathrm{y}} \approx 50$ mBq/cm$^2$ of $^{210}$Po activity three years post-exposure, a $1.8 \times 10^4$ enhancement over ambient; approximately 62% of plated daughters were removable by wiping. Dead-air model predictions matched measurements to within factors of 1–2. For a benchmark $5 \times 5 \times 0.5$ mm$^3$ silicon chip at ambient radon (50 Bq/m$^3$), $^{210}$Pb-chain decays deposit energy at $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$ above 1 MeV, comparable to cosmic-ray protons ($2.1 \times 10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$).
